https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg5l.text: Image source, National Assembly of Zambia Image caption, Mutotwe Kafwaya's death was confirmed days after a raid by security forces Published 20 August 2026, 09:49 BST Updated 2 hours ago By Dingindaba Buyoya Â and Â Basillioh Rukanga A former Zambian minister was killed in last week's raid by security forces on a house linked to opposition leader Brian Mundubile a day after the presidential election, the authorities have said. A police spokesman said Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally wounded by law enforcement officers during what officials have described as an exchange of fire in a security operation in the capital, Lusaka, on Friday. Eleven people were arrested in the raid, with the authorities accusing Mundubile's party, the NRPUP, of being "involved in insurgency" and "militia activity" and storing "high-grade" weapons. Mundubile, who has since gone into hiding, rejected the allegations as "total fabrications". According to official results, incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema won a second five-year term with a 60% share of the vote. Mundubile, who trailed behind with 38%, plans to challenge the outcome in court after alleging the tallying process had been tampered with. Speaking about Kafwaya on Tuesday, the opposition leader said he had had no information of his whereabouts after he had been shot during the raid, which he said took place at his house. The police confirmed Kafwaya's death late on Wednesday amid growing demands for information about him. They said the 49-year-old was killed in a shootout during the raid by a joint security task force, adding that they encountered "gunfire and resistance from unknown individuals, resulting in [them] returning fire". "In the process one unidentified male person was fatally wounded, and the firearm was recovered," the police said, adding that family members had subsequently identified him. Kafwaya first become a lawmaker in 2016 and was appointed by then-President Edgar Lungu as the for minister for works in 2018 and moved to the transport ministry the following year. He served there until 2021, when Lungu lost to Hichilema in the presidential election of that year. He continued serving as an opposition member of parliament. Regional and international observers described the election day as largely peaceful, but raised concerns about late electoral reforms, media freedom and access to the media in the run-up to the poll. The EU election observation mission warned at the weekend that restrictions on the opposition in the campaigning period may have contributed to an "uneven contest". In its report on Wednesday, the observers said the results tabulation process "deteriorated significantly" once counting had resumed after a six-hour pause. The electoral commission halted the count citing violence against its staff and alleging ballot-box theft. The EU mission said staff in many centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced, and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records. It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters. The observers described a heavy military presence as intimidating and said it had received reports of attacks on some tallying centres. It has called for "maximal transparency" over the poll outcome, noting that the electoral commission did not publish separate polling-station results. The Human Rights Commission in Zambia has meanwhile called for accountability over people whose whereabouts remain unknown following arrests and security operations around the elections. It has called for anyone being held beyond the legal period to be taken to court or released, and any alleged unlawful detentions or disappearances to be independently investigated. She is earning up to $180,000 a year as a senior adviser to NSW One Nation senator Sean Bell. Illustration: Josh Agnew/Guardian design The Populist: Pauline Hanson's divided nation One Nation Pauline Hanson’s daughter Lee working for a NSW One Nation senator remotely from Tasmania without ministerial approval Exclusive: Lee Hanson also appears to be regularly campaigning for party during work hours, social media shows Listen to Guardian Australia’s podcast The Populist here Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Sarah Martin Senior correspondent Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Pauline Hanson’s daughter, Lee Hanson, has been working in Tasmania as a senior adviser to a New South Wales One Nation senator without the required ministerial approval, Guardian Australia can reveal. Under work base arrangements that apply to the staff of all MPs, a personal adviser such as Hanson can only be allowed to work in a location other than Canberra or the parliamentarian’s home base with approval from the special minister of state. View image in fullscreen Pauline Hanson with Lee and her son Tony Zagorski at her home during vote counting for the 2004 federal election. Photograph: AAP But Guardian Australia has learned that when Sean Bell appointed her as an adviser, he did not submit a request for an alternative work base arrangement as required under parliamentary rules. The revelations are included in the first episode of The Populist , the Guardian’s new podcast about One Nation. The Department of Finance approved a contract variation for Hanson to be reclassified from an electorate officer to a personal adviser, without going through the proper process. The Populist The Populist: Aeroplanes and bulldozers | Episode 1 Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $ https://audio.guim.co.uk/2026/09/13-33037-THE_POPULIST_E1_AB.mp3 00:00:00 01:01:25 The role pays between $150,000 and $180,000 a year, according to the latest enterprise agreement. Sources say the process was a departmental “stuff-up” that allowed Hanson’s work arrangements to take shape without the minister undertaking the required consideration of “special circumstances” for her employment in a different state. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here A Guardian Australia analysis of Hanson’s social media activity also shows that she appears to be regularly campaigning for One Nation in Tasmania during work hours. If her activities are taking place without taking leave from her role, she would be in breach of the Members of Parliament (Staff) Act, known as the Mops Act. Under the act, staff are employed to assist a parliamentarian to carry out their duties as an MP and “not for party political purposes”. View image in fullscreen The Hansons in a photo from Lee Hanson’s Facebook page Dozens of social media posts and videos on Hanson’s page or One Nation Tasmania’s page in support of her bid to be elected as a senator for the state have been recorded or posted on her site during working hours. It is unclear whether she took leave to attend the events or undertake the campaign-related activities. Hanson has been spearheading the party’s expansion in the state, opening five new branches and claiming thousands of new members. Her Facebook accounts show that while there are almost daily posts about Tasmanian and party issues after work hours, there are many occasions when campaign activity takes place during normal business hours. This includes events that Hanson has attended as a One Nation representative. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Barnaby Joyce says One Nation doesn’t want return of White Australia policy but backs Pauline Hanson on mass deportations Read more In May she opened a new community centre in Longford for the organisation Rekindle. While she posted about the event after hours, the organisation had advertised that she was there during work hours for the ceremony. Hanson also spent a day at AgFest campaigning for the party, rockclimbing with Scouts Tasmania. “Great day meeting locals and enjoying everything AgFest has to offer,” she wrote. After another event, Hanson appears to have confused the day on which a meeting with the group Concerned Farmers Tasmania took place. A social media post for the One Nation Tasmania page on Saturday 16 May said: “Today, I had the pleasure of meeting with several deeply concerned Tasmanian farmers in Ross yesterday.” The Guardian has confirmed that the meeting took place on Friday 15 May. On 5 December last year, also a Friday, Hanson attended a networking event for businesswomen as a party representative, posting about the event with a One Nation authorisation. In February she posted about a “Tassie road trip” with her mother, showing the pair campaigning in regional Tasmania. View image in fullscreen Three of Pauline Hanson’s four children – Adam, Lee and Tony – outside a Brisbane prison after visiting their mother there in 2003. Hanson had been found guilty of electoral fraud but the conviction was later overturned. Photograph: Tony Phillips/EPA Hanson has recorded multiple media interviews about One Nation’s success in Tasmania and posts letters and media releases about state issues. She is also a member of One Nation’s federal executive and oversees the party’s human resources management in parliament. An email obtained by the Guardian was sent to party staff in June announcing the appointment of staff to the MP David Farley’s office. “Please join me in extending a warm welcome to Nicki Waldron and Brenton Trott who have joined David Farley’s parliamentary office,” Hanson says from a party email address sent on a Tuesday afternoon at 2.20pm. “We are still recruiting the remaining positions within David’s office and will therefore make announcements of our new team members in due course. “Please share this with your teams to ensure nobody is missed.” One Nation and Lee Hanson did not reply to questions from Guardian Australia.
